pages.title: Tuval — the board, the page and the work in one place
pages.description: An open-source workspace where an infinite canvas, your documents and your issue tracker are three views of the same records. Run it yourself, or let us keep the disks spinning.
pages.claim: One record. Three ways to look at it.
pages.lede: A sticky on a canvas, a row in a database and an issue in a sprint are usually three tools and three subscriptions. Here they are the same thing, seen from three sides.

bands.heading: This is the editor, not a picture of one
bands.body: Drag something. Nothing here is saved until you say so.

bands.heading: The idea you had on Tuesday is the ticket you close on Friday
bands.body: Select a sticky, turn it into an issue, and it keeps its place on the board while it turns up in the sprint. Nothing is retyped, because nothing was ever copied.

points.title: The whiteboard
points.body: Infinite canvas, frames, connectors, sticky notes, pen, tables, mind maps, templates, presentation mode, comments and live cursors.

points.title: The wiki
points.body: Pages with real blocks, databases with eighteen field types, six views over them, formulas, rollups, relations, publishing and version history.

points.title: The tracker
points.body: Issues with keys, cycles, projects, estimates, labels, sub-issues, blocking relations, a board view and a burn-down.

bands.heading: And it hands the whole thing to an agent
bands.body: A board is already a brief: frames become sections, arrows become a flow, code blocks stay fenced. One button turns a canvas into the prompt you meant to write. An MCP server lets the agent go the other way and read the workspace itself.

bands.heading: Yours either way
bands.body: The code is AGPL. Run it on your own machine and every limit is yours to set. Pay only if you would rather somebody else kept the disks spinning.

pages.title: Infinite canvas — open source whiteboard | Tuval
pages.description: An infinite canvas with frames, connectors, sticky notes, tables and mind maps. Drawn on one canvas element, works offline, and every idea on it can become a tracked issue.
pages.claim: A surface with no edges and no lag.
pages.lede: One canvas element, a dirty-flag render loop, and a document that lives in your browser before it lives anywhere else. Pan, zoom, and keep going.

bands.heading: Try it here
bands.body: Press N for a sticky, L for a connector, P for a pen. Nothing is saved.

bands.heading: The shortcuts you already know
bands.body: V, N, T, S, L, P, F. Marquee select, snap to neighbours, alt-drag to duplicate, space to pan. A tool people have to learn twice is a tool they abandon once.

points.title: Things
points.body: Sticky notes, text, twenty shapes, connectors with labels, freehand pen and highlighter, images, PDFs page by page, tables with merged cells, code blocks, embeds and mind maps that lay themselves out.

points.title: Ways to hold them
points.body: Frames that carry their contents, layers, locking, alignment and distribution, snapping with spacing guides, and a minimap for the far corners.

points.title: People on it
points.body: Live cursors, follow mode, comment pins with threads, and a presentation mode that walks the frames in order.

bands.heading: It works with the network unplugged
bands.body: The document is a CRDT in your browser. The server is where it goes to meet other people, not where it lives.

pages.title: Pages and databases — open source Notion alternative | Tuval
pages.description: Pages with real blocks and databases with eighteen field types, formulas, rollups and relations. Table, board, calendar, gallery, timeline and list views over the same rows.
pages.claim: Write it down. Then ask it questions.
pages.lede: A page is a page until you give it columns. Then it is a database, and the same rows can be a table, a board, a calendar, a gallery or a timeline without being copied.

bands.heading: Eighteen kinds of column
bands.body: Sort it, group it, filter it. This is the real table.

bands.heading: A formula is a column that works out its own answer
bands.body: Add days to a date, roll a related table up into a sum, count what is still open. Created, edited, who by, and the row number are all columns you never have to fill in.

points.title: Blocks
points.body: Headings, lists, toggles, callouts, quotes, code with highlighting, tables, columns, equations in LaTeX, mermaid diagrams, bookmarks, embeds and a table of contents that reads itself from the headings.

points.title: Links between things
points.body: Mention a page and it links; the page you mentioned shows who pointed at it. Mention a person and they hear about it.

points.title: Ways out
points.body: Markdown, HTML, a real text PDF, and a backup of the whole workspace in one file that can be put back.

bands.heading: Collections are questions, not folders
bands.body: Everything of mine that is late. Everything tagged decision. Nothing is filed into a collection and nothing falls out of one when it changes.

pages.title: Issues, cycles and projects — a tracker in your workspace | Tuval
pages.description: Issues with keys, two-week cycles, projects, estimates, labels, sub-issues and blocking relations. In the same workspace as the board the idea came from.
pages.claim: The work, where the thinking already is.
pages.lede: A tracker in a different tab is a tracker somebody forgets to open. This one holds the same records the canvas and the pages hold.

bands.heading: Group it however the question is shaped
bands.body: By status, by person, by priority, by cycle, by project.

bands.heading: A cycle is two weeks of work
bands.body: The next one starts where the last one ended. What did not finish moves, the burn-down says whether it was ever going to, and nobody runs a meeting to find out.

bands.heading: The parts that usually go missing

points.title: Keys that mean something
points.body: TUV-14 is the fourteenth issue in this workspace, taken on insert, never reused, and safe to write in a commit message.

points.title: Relations that read both ways
points.body: This blocks that, so that is blocked by this. Stored once, so the two can never disagree about which way round it is.

points.title: Time, without typing it twice
points.body: Log a stint against an issue and the week adds itself up. Repeating work is asked for every night, so a missed night catches up.

bands.heading: It came from somewhere
bands.body: Select a sticky on a board, turn it into an issue, and the card stays exactly where the thought was. Open the issue and the board is one click away.

pages.title: For software teams — planning, retros and architecture | Tuval
pages.description: Sprint planning, retrospectives, architecture drawings and the issue tracker in one workspace. The sticky from the retro becomes the ticket in the cycle.
pages.claim: The retro sticky and the sprint ticket are the same object.
pages.lede: Most teams run the workshop in one tool and the work in another, then spend an hour moving the first into the second. Skip that hour.

bands.heading: Start where you already start
bands.body: Kanban, retrospective, brainwriting, flowchart, mind map, architecture, five whys.

bands.heading: Monday morning, in order
bands.body: Open last cycle on a board. Drag what did not finish into the next one. Turn the three new stickies into issues without leaving the canvas. Close the tab.

points.title: Planning
points.body: Cycles of two weeks, estimates in points, a burn-down that counts the same set the list shows.

points.title: Design
points.body: Architecture on the canvas, mermaid in the doc, and one button that hands the whole flow to an agent as a brief.

points.title: Afterwards
points.body: A retro board, decisions written down as pages, and an incident record that links to the decision it changed.

bands.heading: The API is a door, not a demo
bands.body: API keys, webhooks and an MCP server, so n8n, a script or a coding agent can read and write the workspace. We integrate rather than clone.

pages.title: For agencies — workshops, delivery and client access | Tuval
pages.description: Run the client workshop on a shared canvas, keep the delivery in the same workspace, and give the client a read-only link without an account.
pages.claim: The client sees the room, not the filing cabinet.
pages.lede: A workshop is worth what survives it. Here the board the client watched being drawn is the same board the work is tracked against.

bands.heading: The room, on a screen everyone can see
bands.body: Live cursors, follow mode, comment pins, presentation mode through the frames.

bands.heading: A link, not an invitation to install something
bands.body: Open a board to anybody with the link and it opens read-only, with no account. Or invite by email, or let a whole email domain in at once.

points.title: The record
points.body: People, companies and deals in a database you did not have to buy a CRM for. A form on a public link drops answers straight into it.

points.title: The delivery
points.body: A project holds its boards, its pages and its issues, and the switch at the top of the sidebar makes everything else disappear until you switch back.

points.title: The proof
points.body: Log time against issues and the week adds itself up, per person, per day.

bands.heading: A booking page, so the meeting books itself
bands.body: Your hours on an address anybody can open. A booking becomes a record like any other.

pages.title: For freelancers — one workspace instead of four | Tuval
pages.description: Notes, client work, invoicing records and the canvas you think on, in one place, for nothing. Run it yourself or use the free plan.
pages.claim: Four subscriptions is three too many.
pages.lede: Working alone does not mean needing less. It means the tax of moving between tools is paid by exactly one person: you.

bands.heading: Think here first
bands.body: The canvas is where the shape of the job turns up before the job does.

bands.heading: Free is not a trial
bands.body: Three people, a gigabyte of files, and every board, page, database and issue there is. No feature is held back to make the paid plan look thin.

bands.heading: The parts of the job nobody bills for

points.title: Keeping track
points.body: A daily journal one keystroke away, a clock against each piece of work, and a week that adds itself up.

points.title: Showing the work
points.body: Publish a page to a public address, or open a board to the world and let a reader copy the brief off it.

points.title: Getting paid attention
points.body: A page of your own with everything you have opened on it, and links to wherever people support your work.

bands.heading: And it is yours
bands.body: AGPL. Download the whole workspace as one file whenever you like, and put it back.

pages.title: For consultants — analysis, findings and handover | Tuval
pages.description: Map the situation on a canvas, keep findings as pages with properties, and hand over a workspace the client can actually keep.
pages.claim: A finding is worth what the client can still read next year.
pages.lede: The deliverable is usually a deck nobody opens twice. This is the alternative: a workspace that stays readable, searchable and exportable after you leave.

bands.heading: Map it before you write it
bands.body: Five whys, customer journey, architecture. The templates are there.

bands.heading: A finding is a record, not a slide
bands.body: Give it a status, an owner, a date and a tag. Then a collection answers "everything still open" for the rest of the engagement without anybody maintaining a list.

points.title: Decisions with their reasons
points.body: What was chosen, what it was chosen instead of, and why. Linked to the incident that prompted it.

points.title: Everything, in one file
points.body: A backup of every page, issue, database, tag and link, which can be restored into their own workspace, self-hosted, with no licence to buy.

points.title: Or a real PDF
points.body: Text you can select and search, not a screenshot of a document.

bands.heading: Read-only means read-only
bands.body: Viewer access is enforced in the database, not hidden in the interface. A viewer who opens the console still cannot write.

pages.title: Self-hosting — run the whole workspace yourself | Tuval
pages.description: AGPL-3.0. Run Tuval on your own machine with your own Postgres and storage. Every limit is yours to set, and the data never leaves.
pages.claim: Your machine. Your database. Your problem, and that is the point.
pages.lede: The hosted plan is a convenience, not a lock. The same code that runs the hosted one is the code you can run, and there is no edition with the good parts missing.

points.title: A Postgres
points.body: Supabase, or a plain Postgres with the same extensions. The schema is a folder of migrations you can read before you run them.

points.title: Somewhere for files
points.body: Any S3-compatible bucket. Images and attachments are signed URLs, never public ones.

points.title: A static host
points.body: The app builds to a folder of files. Anything that can serve them will do.

bands.heading: Nothing is held back
bands.body: No enterprise edition, no feature flags, no telemetry. The limits on the hosted plan are seats and disk, because those are what cost money to serve. Run it yourself and you set both.

bands.heading: Access is decided by the database
bands.body: Every rule about who may read or write what is a row-level security policy, proven by a suite of access checks that runs against the real schema before any change ships. An interface that hides a button is not security; this is.

bands.heading: And you can leave
bands.body: One file holds every page, issue, database, tag and link, and restores into any workspace.

pages.title: Pricing — free for small teams, paid to be hosted | Tuval
pages.description: Free for up to three people with every feature. The paid plan is for people who would rather not run the servers. The code is AGPL and self-hosting is unlimited.
pages.claim: The code is free. The disks are not.
pages.lede: What is priced here is somebody else running it: the disks, the bandwidth and the answering. So what is limited is what actually costs money to serve, and nothing else.

points.title: Up to three people
points.body: Everybody in the workspace, not per board.

points.title: A gigabyte of files
points.body: Images, PDFs and attachments across the workspace.

points.title: Every feature
points.body: Every board, page, database and issue. Publishing, forms and booking links included.

bands.heading: Team
bands.body: As many people as you like, ten gigabytes of files for each of them, and the API and webhooks so n8n and the rest can reach it. Everything on the free plan as well.

bands.heading: Or none of the above
bands.body: Run it on your own machine and every limit here is yours to set. That is not a downgrade path; it is the same code.
